MG EV Project

Electric vehicle tinkering, charging, data and home-energy curiosity around the MG EV.

Not written up yet

The car turned out to be the small part.

Living with an electric car and being unable to leave it alone. Charging behaviour, home energy data, and the slow realisation that the interesting system spans vehicle, charger, tariff and house. There is a half-formed smart-lead project in here too: ESP32, a custom circuit board, and enough sensing to make the charging cable part of the system rather than a dumb object lying on the floor.

Smart lead

The connector rabbit hole.

The cable work got practical quickly: Duosida Type 2 contacts, CP/PP signal pins, 2.5mm and 6mm power conductors, and whether the right answer was a ratchet crimper, a hydraulic crimper, or solder. For a one-off prototype the important parts are not glamorous: strain relief, no solder wicking into a flex point, a pull test, then staged current tests with temperature checks before trusting it at 32A.

Design direction

Make the cable observable.

The interesting idea is still the ESP32/controller side: treat the charging lead as part of the home-energy system, with enough electronics to know what is happening instead of just assuming the cable is a passive thing between the car and the wall.

Bench testing

The fake car.

A useful side quest was not a fake battery, but a fake EV: a small Type 2 test box that can present the charger with the right CP and PP behaviour without needing the car on the drive. For AC charging that means selectable pilot states, a diode check, cable-rating resistors, and a way of showing what current the charger is actually advertising.

IEC 61851

One wire doing two jobs.

The control pilot is pleasingly robust engineering: a 1kHz signal tells the car the available current by duty cycle, while the voltage level tells the charger whether a vehicle is connected and ready. A little ESP32 analyser could display pilot state, duty cycle and advertised current, which is exactly the kind of thing that turns a confusing charging problem into something observable.

Fault finding

When the charger says GFCI.

The OpenEVSE debugging was classic physical-system work: the car was detected, the contactor closed, then the GFCI fault appeared. That points away from the logic layer and towards the power path: Live and Neutral through the differential toroid exactly once, Earth and CP/PP outside it, then continuity and isolation checks before blaming anything clever.
